sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Tampere prices its street parking in three zones and is now reshaping the policy to 2040. The city's payment-zone page, updated on 16 September 2026, lists zone 1 at 3.50 euros an hour with a two-hour limit, zone 2 at 2.20 euros with four hours and zone 3 at 1.40 euros with ten hours; zone 1 costs half on Sundays and holidays and zones 2 and 3 are free then [1]. Yle reported in December 2024 a proposal to raise prices by about 10 percent from 1 February, to those levels, the first rise since 2019, and that the city did not intend to cut fees for fully electric cars [2]. Resident permits in zones A to K cost 25 euros a month or 300 a year [3]. The city issued 58,649 parking charges in 2025, down from 68,774 in 2023, worth 4.6 million euros, and has over 4,000 paid street spaces [5].

On 15 June 2026, according to Yle, the city board approved the parking policy to 2040. It mentions progressive street pricing in the busiest central shopping streets, recommends that the street price reach the underground car-park price at 30 minutes and recommends stricter time limits for the payment zones; the city is next to draw up a plan [0]. The March 2025 draft compared permits issued in January 2024 with street spaces: permits equalled 101 percent of spaces in zone A and 100 percent in zone D, against 32 percent in zone K; the table calls it utilisation, but it is permits per space, not measured occupancy [4]. A 2022 city-centre study counted 41,750 car spaces in the study area, including 18 car parks with 8,150 spaces, and about 58 percent of households there have no car [6].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The development is underground. The city's page of May 2026 says the aim is to move street-level capacity phase by phase into underground facilities, with the Viinikankatu connection built together with the first extension of the P-Hämppi garage; construction of the Yliopistontunneli access tunnel started in May [14]. In February 2026 a design team was chosen for the Viinikankatu access road and the P-Hämppi extension, a project that continues into the 2030s [13]. On park and ride, Yle reported in March 2026 that Hiedanranta, with 130 spaces, was full by about 9 a.m. on two of three observed weekday mornings, and that an extension with 90 more spaces was expected by autumn 2026 [15]; Nysse's page now lists Hiedanranta with 220 spaces, but is undated and does not prove completion [16]. Tram line 1 started running to Lentävänniemi in January 2025, with extensions to Pirkkala and Ruotula under way [17].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The city lists car park operators Aimo Park, EuroPark, Finnpark, Pyynikin Trikoon parkki and Sokos, and says the list is not complete [7]. Finnpark, owned by the City of Tampere, extended resident parking from five to nine central halls in September 2026 [10], and reports a survey of 3,587 of its app customers with 90 percent satisfied, a self-selected sample [11]. P-Hämppi has 972 spaces at 4.20 euros an hour for the first three hours and a 35-euro daily maximum [8], with 39 charging points [12]. Finnpark announced a two-month pilot of half-price Sundays in P-Hämppi in October and November 2026 [9]. Nysse's park-and-ride page lists Hiedanranta, Niihama, Kaukajärvi and Koivistonkylä, with workday parking free [16].

Our data cover two park-and-rides, Hiedanranta (126 spaces in the feed) and Niihama (72), measured since 27 September 2026. Occupancy averaged about 47% on weekdays and 30% at weekends, weighted by spaces. Both reached full or nearly full in single readings, Hiedanranta on a Monday morning at 08:00, which fits Yle's account of the morning pressure. Neither is a city-centre garage, so these figures do not describe the underground facilities the city plans to build. About four weeks of data.
